brick: The Central Dogma: DNA to RNA to Proteins
explanation: The 5' cap (7-methylguanosine linked 5'-to-5') stabilizes the transcript against exonucleases and is recognized by initiation factors to promote translation.

brick: The Central Dogma: DNA to RNA to Proteins
explanation: The spliceosome (built from snRNPs) cleaves at the 5' and 3' splice sites, excises the intron as a lariat, and ligates the two exons, an essential step in mRNA maturation.

brick: The Central Dogma: DNA to RNA to Proteins
explanation: Alternative splicing joins different combinations of exons from the same primary transcript, so one gene can encode several protein isoforms, greatly expanding proteome diversity.

brick: The Central Dogma: DNA to RNA to Proteins
explanation: Incoming aminoacyl-tRNAs enter the A site; the growing peptide is held at the P site and transferred to the A-site amino acid, after which deacylated tRNA leaves through the E site.

brick: The Central Dogma: DNA to RNA to Proteins
explanation: The cloverleaf molecule is a tRNA. When 'charged,' an amino acid is esterified to its 3' acceptor end; its anticodon then reads the complementary mRNA codon (with wobble at the third position), delivering the correct amino acid to the ribosomal A site during translation.

brick: BOOM: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I
explanation: The central (alpha) carbon bonded to an amino group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen, and a variable R side chain is the defining structure of an amino acid. The R group distinguishes the 20 standard amino acids; the charged groups reflect the zwitterionic form at physiologic pH.

brick: BOOM: Proteins, Enzymatic Machines and Introduction to Protein-based Disorders I
explanation: The peptide bond forms by condensation: the carboxyl group of one amino acid joins the amino group of the next, releasing one water molecule (dehydration synthesis). The reverse, hydrolysis, breaks the bond by adding water.

brick: BOOM: Lipids and Lipid Metabolism Introduction
explanation: A fatty acid has a hydrophobic tail and a hydrophilic (charged) carboxylate head, making it amphipathic. This property lets fatty acids and their derivatives form micelles and membrane bilayers.

brick: BOOM: Lipids and Lipid Metabolism Introduction
explanation: The three ketone bodies are acetoacetate, acetone, and beta-hydroxybutyrate. Beta-hydroxybutyrate carries a hydroxyl (not a carbonyl/ketone) group, so it is chemically not a ketone, even though it is counted as a ketone body.
A ringed sideroblast is an erythroid precursor with iron-laden mitochondria forming a perinuclear ring (Prussian blue positive), diagnostic of sideroblastic anemia.
Mitosis produces two daughter cells that are diploid (2n) and genetically identical to the parent, in contrast to meiosis which yields four genetically unique haploid cells.
